whatIsRationality.title: What is rationality?
whatIsRationality.intro: Rationality is the ability to form beliefs that accurately reflect reality (epistemic rationality) and make decisions that maximize your goals (instrumental rationality).
whatIsRationality.improvable: While intelligence (IQ) measures cognitive capacity, rationality measures how effectively you use that capacity. Whether rational thinking can be lastingly improved remains scientifically debated, although some targeted interventions show short-term effects.
whatIsRationality.testDescription: This test evaluates several key dimensions of rational thinking: probabilistic reasoning, scientific reasoning, resistance to
whatIsRationality.andUpdating: , and the ability to update your beliefs in light of new evidence.

probabilistic.title: 🎲 Probabilistic Reasoning
probabilistic.description: Your ability to reason correctly with probabilities and avoid classic errors such as:
probabilistic.baseRateDesc: Underestimating the importance of general statistics
probabilistic.gamblersDesc: Believing that past events influence future probabilities in random situations
probabilistic.conjunctionDesc: Thinking that two events together are more probable than one alone

scientific.title: 🔬 Scientific Reasoning
scientific.description: Your ability to test hypotheses rigorously:
scientific.falsificationDesc: Seeking evidence that could refute a hypothesis
scientific.correlationDesc: Understanding that correlation does not necessarily imply causation
scientific.controlDesc: Recognizing the importance of appropriate comparisons

reflection.title: 🧠 Reflection vs Intuition
reflection.description: Your ability to override immediate intuitive responses (which are often incorrect) to engage deeper analytical thinking. Based on the
reflection.exampleQuestion: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?

biases.title: ⚖️ Reasoning Biases

biases.beliefDesc: Letting your prior beliefs influence your evaluation of logic
biases.framingDesc: Changing your mind depending on how information is presented
biases.anchoringDesc: Being too influenced by the first piece of information received

rational.title: 🔮 Rational vs Irrational Thinking

results.criticalNoteText: Knowing your biases does not eliminate them. Even Daniel Kahneman (2002 Nobel Prize for his work on biases) admitted: "I have learned a great deal about cognitive biases, but I am not sure I have become less susceptible to these biases." The real solution? Change your decision environment (checklists, protocols, third-party consultation), not just yourself.

interpretations.excellent: Excellent level of rationality. You demonstrate strong critical thinking skills across most dimensions. You are able to resist common cognitive biases and reason rigorously.
interpretations.good: Good level of rationality. You have solid reasoning skills but there is room for improvement in certain areas. Some cognitive biases still influence your judgments.

moduleDescriptions.Probabilistic Reasoning: Your ability to reason with probabilities and avoid classic errors (gambler's fallacy, base rate neglect, conjunction error).
moduleDescriptions.Scientific Reasoning: Your ability to rigorously test hypotheses, falsify rather than confirm, and distinguish correlation from causation.
moduleDescriptions.Reflection vs Intuition: Your ability to inhibit the immediate intuitive response and engage analytical reflection (CRT).
moduleDescriptions.Belief Bias: Your ability to evaluate logical validity independently of your beliefs about the conclusion.
moduleDescriptions.Knowledge Calibration: Your ability to accurately estimate your level of certainty (avoid overconfidence).
moduleDescriptions.Probabilistic Numeracy: Your ability to manipulate numbers in probabilistic contexts and understand statistics.
moduleDescriptions.Superstitious Thinking: Your resistance to paranormal/supernatural beliefs and respect for the principle 'belief proportional to evidence'.
moduleDescriptions.Anti-Science Attitudes: Your resistance to rejecting science and the scientific method.
moduleDescriptions.Conspiracy Beliefs: Your resistance to conspiracy explanations and ability to apply Occam's Razor.
moduleDescriptions.Disjunctive Reasoning: Your ability to reason correctly with 'OR' statements.
moduleDescriptions.Anchoring: Your resistance to anchoring (being too influenced by the first piece of information received).
moduleDescriptions.Dysfunctional Beliefs: Your ability to avoid irrational beliefs that cause unnecessary emotional distress.
moduleDescriptions.Argument Evaluation: Your ability to evaluate argument strength independently of your personal opinions (resistance to belief bias in argumentation).
moduleDescriptions.Causal Reasoning: Your ability to distinguish correlation from causation and recognize the importance of control groups in experiments.
moduleDescriptions.Framing Effects: Your resistance to framing effects: giving consistent answers regardless of how information is presented (positive vs negative framing).
moduleDescriptions.Sensitivity to Expected Value: Your ability to rationally choose between bets by maximizing expected value rather than following intuitions.
moduleDescriptions.Sunk Cost Fallacy: Your resistance to the sunk cost fallacy: not letting past investments influence future decisions.

scoreInterpretations.exceptional: Exceptional score (top 1%). You belong to the elite of rational thinking. However, knowing about biases doesn't guarantee resisting them in real situations (fatigue, stress, emotions). Even at the highest levels, using decision-making protocols remains crucial for important choices.
scoreInterpretations.veryHigh: Very high score (top 5%). You demonstrate solid mastery of rational thinking principles. Keep practicing and stay vigilant: biases can still manifest in new or stressful situations.
scoreInterpretations.high: High score (top 16%). You've developed a good understanding of common reasoning errors and can identify them. Biases persist even in experts: using protocols and external tools remains recommended for your important decisions.
scoreInterpretations.aboveAverage: Above average score (top 32%). You're on the right track. You already identify several common biases. Now focus on your specific weaknesses visible in the module details to progress further.
scoreInterpretations.average: Average score (40th-60th percentile). You correctly identify some biases, but others still escape you. This is normal: rationality isn't intuitive. Focus on your specific weaknesses rather than trying to improve everything at once.
scoreInterpretations.slightlyBelow: Slightly below average score (25th-40th percentile). Several cognitive biases affect your reasoning. Improvement is possible with deliberate practice. Identify your main weaknesses and work on them methodically.
scoreInterpretations.belowAverage: Significantly below average score (10th-25th percentile). Many important cognitive biases affect your reasoning. Prioritize using external tools (checklists, protocols, consultations) to compensate for these biases in your important decisions. Improvement requires time and practice (6-12 months minimum).
scoreInterpretations.limited: Low score (bottom 10%). Your results suggest strong susceptibility to common cognitive biases. Be reassured: even very intelligent people get similar scores without training. Rationality works differently from intelligence. Start by understanding basic concepts well before expecting measurable improvement.

testOrigin.title: 📖 About This Test
testOrigin.cartDescription: The Comprehensive Assessment of Rational Thinking (CART) is the first scientifically validated test of rational thinking, developed by Professors Keith E. Stanovich, Richard F. West, and Maggie E. Toplak, published by MIT Press in 2016.
testOrigin.basedOnResearch: Based on 40 years of research in cognitive psychology on biases and heuristics, notably the pioneering work of Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky (Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002 for this work).
testOrigin.adaptationDescription: This test is a free educational adaptation of CART. It uses public domain questions and variants inspired by the scientific literature. This is NOT the official CART (which requires controlled administration), but a free pedagogical approximation.
testOrigin.keyDifference: Key difference: Intelligence (IQ) measures your cognitive capacity, but rationality measures how effectively you use that capacity. You can be intelligent but not very rational.

cartHistory.title: 📖 Where Does This Test Come From? CART History
cartHistory.fortyYearsP1: In the 1970s, two Israeli psychologists, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky (Hebrew University of Jerusalem), began documenting something troubling: intelligent, educated people regularly made decisions that violated basic principles of logic and probability.
cartHistory.fortyYearsP2: Their most surprising discovery? These errors were not random accidents, but systematic patterns. Humans seemed to use mental shortcuts (heuristics) which, although useful in some contexts, led to predictable and repeated errors.
cartHistory.fortyYearsP3: For this pioneering work, Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002 (Tversky had died in 1996, otherwise he would have shared it).
cartHistory.theProblemP1: For decades, it was assumed that IQ tests measured "good thinking". But Keith E. Stanovich (University of Toronto) noticed something strange in the 1990s: people with very high IQs still made systematic reasoning errors.
cartHistory.theProblemP2: Stanovich realized that IQ measures the brain's processing power, but not necessarily the wisdom of its use. It's like having a Ferrari (high IQ) but not knowing how to drive (low rationality).
cartHistory.birthOfCartP1: Stanovich, along with his colleagues Richard F. West (James Madison University) and Maggie E. Toplak (York University), spent 3 years developing the CART (Comprehensive Assessment of Rational Thinking) - the first comprehensive test of rational thinking.
cartHistory.birthOfCartP2: The project, funded by the John Templeton Foundation, involved over 1000 participants, 20 different subtests, and rigorous statistical validation.
cartHistory.birthOfCartP3: This online test is a free educational adaptation of the original CART. It uses public domain questions and variants inspired by the scientific literature. This is NOT the official CART (which requires controlled administration), but a free pedagogical approximation.

pragmaticSolution.title: 🛠️ The Pragmatic Solution (Recommended by Kahneman)
pragmaticSolution.intro: Rather than trying to change your brain (difficult, uncertain), change your decision-making environment:
pragmaticSolution.checklist: Pre-decision checklists: "What is the base rate? Am I anchored? What could prove me wrong?"
pragmaticSolution.consultation: Structured consultations: Before any major decision, get input from 2-3 people with different perspectives
pragmaticSolution.slowdown: Forced slowdown: 24-48h rule for important decisions (investments, major purchases, career changes)
pragmaticSolution.premortem: Pre-mortem: Before launching a project, imagine it failed in 1 year. Why?
pragmaticSolution.journal: Decision journal: Write down predictions + confidence + reasoning. Monthly review.
pragmaticSolution.example: Concrete example: In surgery, enforcing a mandatory checklist reduced complications by 47% (Haynes et al., 2009) - much more effective than "training surgeons to be less overconfident".

stateOfResearch.title: 🔬 Where are we now? Current state of rationality research
stateOfResearch.intro: An honest assessment of what we know, what we don't know, and what remains contentious:
stateOfResearch.finding1: Cognitive biases are real and robust
stateOfResearch.finding1Text: Hundreds of studies confirm systematic reasoning errors across populations. These are not laboratory artifacts—they manifest in medical decisions, financial choices, legal judgments, and everyday reasoning.
stateOfResearch.finding2Text: IQ and rational thinking are only modestly correlated (r ≈ 0.30-0.40). High-IQ individuals frequently exhibit severe cognitive biases. CART successfully measures reasoning abilities distinct from traditional intelligence tests.
stateOfResearch.finding3Text: A 2025 meta-analysis of 54 randomized controlled trials found small but significant improvements from educational interventions (g = 0.26). Even brief training (videos, games) can reduce biases like anchoring and confirmation bias—but effects are modest and require reinforcement.
stateOfResearch.question1Text: Training improves performance on specific tasks but rarely generalizes to novel contexts. Why don't debiasing skills transfer? We lack a clear theoretical account. Most interventions fail outside laboratory conditions.
stateOfResearch.question2: How do System 1 and System 2 actually interact?
stateOfResearch.question2Text: The dual-process framework (intuitive vs. analytical thinking) faces serious criticisms: oversimplification, unfalsifiability, vague definitions. Critics argue it's too simplistic and can't explain the complex interplay between intuitive and deliberate processes. The field lacks consensus.
stateOfResearch.question3Text: Effects often dissipate within days without practice. We don't know how to achieve lasting behavioral change at acceptable cost. Real-world evidence of sustained improvement remains scarce.
stateOfResearch.question4: Does bias awareness translate to better decisions?
stateOfResearch.question4Text: A troubling gap: reducing measured bias doesn't consistently improve real-world outcomes. Meta-analyses find weak or zero effects on actual discrimination and decision quality. Awareness ≠ behavioral change.
stateOfResearch.controversy1Text: Critics argue CART and similar tests reflect WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) assumptions. Is probabilistic reasoning "more rational" than other cultural reasoning styles, or just different? No resolution yet.
stateOfResearch.controversy2Text: Some studies find experts more susceptible to certain biases (motivated reasoning, overconfidence in their domain). Others find expertise protective. Context dependency makes generalizations risky.
stateOfResearch.controversy3Text: A 2021 study found serious dimensionality issues with short-form CART: many subtests failed to form coherent scales. Abbreviated versions (like this test) sacrifice validity for accessibility.
stateOfResearch.bottomLine1: ✅ Rationality research has produced robust findings about systematic reasoning errors and ways to measure them.
stateOfResearch.bottomLine2: ⚠️ We have limited understanding of how to produce lasting, generalizable improvements in rational thinking.
stateOfResearch.bottomLine3: ❌ Many fundamental questions remain unresolved—especially about real-world transfer and the mechanisms underlying rational thought.
stateOfResearch.bottomLine4: 🔬 Active area of research with a 2024 adolescent assessment tool (ART-Y) and ongoing meta-analyses, but no breakthroughs solving the transfer problem.
stateOfResearch.bottomLine5: 🎯 Practical recommendation: Use external decision protocols (checklists, consultations, systematic review processes) rather than relying on internalized debiasing.
stateOfResearch.recentWorkText: New measurement tools for youth (ART-Y, 2024), meta-analyses on educational interventions showing modest effects, but fundamental challenges—transfer, durability, real-world impact—remain largely unsolved.

methodology.title: Methodology & Scientific Validation
methodology.subtitle: Understanding the scientific foundations of this rationality test

cartSection.title: What is CART?
cartSection.description: The Comprehensive Assessment of Rational Thinking (CART) is a scientifically validated test battery developed by cognitive psychologists Keith E. Stanovich, Richard F. West, and Maggie E. Toplak. Published by MIT Press in 2016, it represents over 40 years of research on rational thinking and cognitive biases.
cartSection.purposeText: Unlike IQ tests that measure cognitive capacity, CART evaluates how effectively individuals use their reasoning abilities in real-world situations. It assesses susceptibility to cognitive biases, probabilistic reasoning, scientific thinking, and belief updating.

validationSection.title: Scientific Validation
validationSection.psychometricText: CART has been rigorously validated across multiple studies with thousands of participants. It demonstrates strong reliability (test-retest correlation > 0.80) and validity in predicting real-world decision-making outcomes.
validationSection.independenceText: Research shows that CART measures abilities distinct from general intelligence (IQ). While IQ and rationality are modestly correlated (r ≈ 0.30-0.40), rational thinking explains unique variance in life outcomes beyond what IQ predicts.
validationSection.realWorldText: CART scores predict important life outcomes including:
validationSection.outcome2: Reduced susceptibility to scams and manipulation
validationSection.outcome3: More accurate beliefs about important topics

adaptationSection.title: Our Adaptation
adaptationSection.description: This test is an educational adaptation of CART principles. We use:
adaptationSection.item1: Public domain questions from the cognitive psychology literature
adaptationSection.item2: Original variants inspired by published research
adaptationSection.item3: Validated question types from multiple studies
adaptationSection.difference1: Shorter format (20-90 min vs. 3+ hours for full CART)
adaptationSection.difference3: Educational focus (learning tool vs. research instrument)

limitationsSection.title: Limitations & Critiques
limitationsSection.limitation1Text: Research shows that knowing about cognitive biases doesn't automatically eliminate them. Even experts remain susceptible to the biases they study.
limitationsSection.limitation2Text: Rational thinking performance varies by domain and context. Someone might reason well about health decisions but poorly about financial ones.
limitationsSection.limitation3Text: Many rationality assessments reflect Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) cultural assumptions about 'correct' reasoning.
limitationsSection.limitation4Text: Test scores depend heavily on motivation and cognitive effort. A low score might reflect low engagement rather than low ability.
limitationsSection.limitation5Text: This test is educational, not diagnostic. It cannot identify clinical conditions or definitively measure your 'rationality quotient'.

improvementSection.title: Can Rationality Be Improved?
improvementSection.method1Text: Training in probabilistic reasoning, scientific thinking, and bias awareness can improve performance on rationality tests.
improvementSection.method2Text: The most effective improvements come from using checklists, decision protocols, and consultation processes—not from willpower alone.
improvementSection.method3Text: Skills often don't transfer automatically across domains. Practice reasoning about statistics won't necessarily improve social judgment.
improvementSection.realisticText: Improvement is possible but typically modest. Don't expect dramatic changes. The goal is incremental progress and better decision-making tools, not cognitive transformation.
